course.title: Microbiology
course.description: Microbiology is the study of the organisms too small to see with the unaided eye - bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists, and viruses - and of how they live, grow, cause disease, and shape the world around us. This course moves from the history of the field and the germ theory of disease through microbial cells, growth, genetics, and control, to infection, immunity, antibiotics, and the resistance crisis. Structure and topics are adapted from the Microbiology article on Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: Who is often credited as the first to observe living microorganisms through a microscope?
questions.explanation: Van Leeuwenhoek described swarming 'animalcules' in the 1670s using his handmade lenses - see 'Microbiology and its history'.

questions.prompt: The germ theory of disease states that...
options: diseases arise from bad air alone
many diseases are caused by microorganisms
questions.explanation: Germ theory links many illnesses to microorganisms that can pass between hosts.

questions.prompt: Which group of organisms lacks a membrane-bound nucleus?
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) keep their DNA loose in the cytoplasm with no nucleus.

questions.prompt: A virus differs from a bacterium because a virus...
options: cannot reproduce without a host cell
questions.explanation: A virus is not a cell; it must hijack a host cell to make new particles.

questions.prompt: Autoclaving achieves sterilization mainly through...
questions.explanation: An autoclave uses pressurized steam near 121 degrees Celsius to kill even spores.

questions.prompt: Horizontal gene transfer in bacteria includes...
questions.explanation: These three routes move genes between cells without ordinary reproduction.

questions.prompt: Antimicrobial resistance spreads faster when antibiotics are...
questions.explanation: Overuse and misuse select for resistant microbes and let resistance genes spread.

questions.prompt: Which process carried out by nitrogen-fixing microbes benefits plants?
options: converting nitrogen gas into usable compounds
questions.explanation: Nitrogen fixation turns atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants can take up.

lessons.title: Microbiology and its history
lessons.grammar_note: Names are romanized without accents here: 'van Leeuwenhoek', 'Pasteur', 'Koch'. The words 'microbe' and 'microorganism' mean the same thing.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Define microbiology, say what counts as a microbe, and name the people and ideas that turned curiosity about tiny life into a science. You will be able to explain the germ theory of disease and why it mattered for medicine and public health. Warm-up: before microscopes existed, why was it so hard to explain how infectious diseases spread from person to person?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Microbiology is the study of microorganisms - living things too small to see with the unaided eye - together with the viruses, which are not cells at all. It includes bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists, and viruses, and it asks how they live, grow, interact, and affect larger organisms. The field opened in the 1670s when Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch cloth merchant and lens grinder, used handmade microscopes to describe swarming 'animalcules' in pond water, rainwater, and the scrapings from his own teeth. For nearly two hundred years no one knew what these creatures did. In the 1860s Louis Pasteur showed that specific microbes drive fermentation and spoilage and that gentle heating can slow them, a process now called pasteurization. He also helped overturn the old idea of spontaneous generation. Robert Koch then tied particular microbes to particular diseases. From this work came the germ theory of disease: the understanding that many illnesses are caused by microorganisms that can move from one host to another.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment is a classic. He boiled broth in a flask with a long, curved neck that let air in but trapped dust and microbes in the bend. The broth stayed clear for a long time; when he tipped it so the liquid touched the neck, it quickly clouded with growth. This showed that microbes come from other microbes in the air, not from the broth itself. Koch worked out a practical test for cause, now called Koch's postulates: the microbe must be found in sick hosts, grown in pure culture, cause the disease when introduced into a healthy host, and then be recovered again. To do this he developed pure-culture methods and staining, growing single colonies on solid media so one species could be studied alone. Using these tools he identified the bacteria behind anthrax, tuberculosis, and cholera. Pasteur, meanwhile, developed early vaccines for fowl cholera, anthrax, and rabies by weakening the agents that cause them.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Who first described living microorganisms, and roughly when? 2) What idea did Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment help disprove? 3) State the core claim of the germ theory of disease in one sentence. 4) Why did Koch grow microbes in pure culture? 5) Name one disease whose cause Koch identified. Answers: 1) Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, in the 1670s. 2) Spontaneous generation - the idea that life arises on its own from nonliving matter. 3) Many diseases are caused by microorganisms that can pass from host to host. 4) So he could study one species at a time and be sure which microbe caused what. 5) Anthrax, tuberculosis, or cholera.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: thinking all microbes cause disease. In fact most are harmless or helpful, and only a minority are pathogens. Mistake: treating viruses as ordinary cells - they are acellular and reproduce only inside a host. Exit ticket: (a) What is the germ theory of disease? (b) What are Koch's postulates used to establish? Answers: (a) The understanding that many diseases are caused by microorganisms that spread between hosts. (b) That a specific microbe is the cause of a specific disease, by finding it, growing it in pure culture, reproducing the disease, and recovering it again.

lessons.title: The microbial world
lessons.grammar_note: Prokaryote means a cell with no membrane-bound nucleus (bacteria and archaea); eukaryote means a cell that has one (fungi, protists, plants, animals).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Sort the major groups of microbes - bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists, and viruses - and say how each is built and how it makes more of itself. You will be able to explain why viruses sit apart from the others. Warm-up: which of these groups is not made of cells at all?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The microbial world spans several very different kinds of life. Bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes: they have no nucleus, and they reproduce by splitting in two, called binary fission. They live almost everywhere - soil, water, skin, and gut. Archaea look similar under a microscope but form a separate domain with distinct chemistry; many thrive in extreme heat, salt, or acid, though plenty live in ordinary places too. Fungi are eukaryotes with a nucleus and include single-celled yeasts and multicellular molds; they absorb nutrients and often reproduce by spores. Protists are a mixed group of eukaryotes that are neither plants, animals, nor fungi, such as amoebae, paramecia, and the parasite that causes malaria. Viruses stand apart: they are not cells but packages of genetic material, DNA or RNA, inside a protein coat. A virus cannot grow or copy itself alone; it must hijack a living host cell to make new virus particles. Because of this, biologists still debate whether viruses are truly alive.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Scientists tell these groups apart with a mix of tools. The Gram stain splits bacteria into Gram-positive and Gram-negative based on their cell walls, which look purple or pink after staining. Microscopy reveals shape - round cocci, rod-shaped bacilli, and spiral forms. Culturing on selective media lets one species grow while others are held back. Today, sequencing of ribosomal RNA genes places microbes on the tree of life and revealed archaea as a domain of their own, in work led by Carl Woese. Examples help: Escherichia coli is a rod-shaped gut bacterium; the yeast Saccharomyces is used in bread and beer; Plasmodium is the protist behind malaria; and influenza and the common cold are caused by viruses. Molds such as Penicillium gave us the first antibiotics, showing that even within one group the range of effects is huge.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Do bacteria have a nucleus? 2) Which two groups make up the prokaryotes? 3) Why can a virus not reproduce on its own? 4) Give one example of a protist and what it does. 5) What does the Gram stain distinguish? Answers: 1) No; bacteria are prokaryotes. 2) Bacteria and archaea. 3) It is not a cell and has no machinery of its own, so it must use a host cell. 4) Plasmodium, which causes malaria (amoeba or paramecium are also fine). 5) Gram-positive from Gram-negative bacteria, based on cell-wall structure.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: lumping archaea in with bacteria - they look alike but are a separate domain with different biochemistry. Mistake: calling a virus a kind of cell or assuming it grows like a bacterium; a virus has no cell and cannot multiply outside a host. Exit ticket: (a) Name the five broad groups of microbes covered here. (b) What is the key difference between a prokaryote and a eukaryote? Answers: (a) Bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists, and viruses. (b) A eukaryote has a membrane-bound nucleus; a prokaryote does not.

lessons.title: Prokaryotic cells, growth, and metabolism
lessons.grammar_note: Binary fission is asexual: one cell becomes two identical cells. 'Generation time' is how long that doubling takes.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe the parts of a prokaryotic cell, explain how microbial populations grow, and sort microbes by how they get energy and carbon. You will be able to read a bacterial growth curve and name the main types of metabolism. Warm-up: if one bacterium divides every 30 minutes, how many are there after 2 hours?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A typical prokaryotic cell is small and simple compared with a eukaryotic one. Its DNA sits loose in the cytoplasm as a single circular chromosome in a region called the nucleoid, with no surrounding membrane. Most bacteria have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan outside the cell membrane, and many add an outer capsule for protection. Some carry whip-like flagella for movement and short pili for attachment or gene transfer. Small rings of extra DNA called plasmids often ride along and can carry useful genes. Microbes grow by binary fission, and a population in rich conditions follows a growth curve: a lag phase while cells adjust, an exponential or log phase of rapid doubling, a stationary phase as nutrients run low, and a death phase. Because growth is exponential, numbers climb astonishingly fast when food and space allow, which is why a small contamination can spoil food overnight.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: Microbes are grouped by their energy and carbon sources. Phototrophs capture light; chemotrophs get energy from chemical reactions. Autotrophs build their own carbon compounds from carbon dioxide, while heterotrophs take in organic carbon made by others. Many pathogens are chemoheterotrophs. Oxygen use also varies: obligate aerobes need oxygen, obligate anaerobes are poisoned by it, and facultative anaerobes use it when present but can live without it. Metabolism includes aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration, and fermentation, which yields less energy but needs no oxygen - this is how yeast makes alcohol and how bacteria sour milk into yogurt. For example, with a 30-minute generation time, one cell becomes about a million in roughly 10 hours. Temperature matters too; mesophiles favor body temperature, while thermophiles prefer heat, which is one reason refrigeration slows spoilage.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Where is the DNA in a prokaryotic cell? 2) Name the four phases of the bacterial growth curve in order. 3) What is a plasmid? 4) What does a facultative anaerobe do with oxygen? 5) An autotroph gets its carbon from what? Answers: 1) In the nucleoid, as a circular chromosome with no membrane around it. 2) Lag, exponential (log), stationary, and death. 3) A small ring of extra DNA separate from the main chromosome, often carrying useful genes. 4) It uses oxygen when available but can also grow without it. 5) Carbon dioxide, which it fixes into organic compounds.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: picturing bacterial growth as steady rather than exponential; doubling means numbers explode quickly in the log phase. Mistake: assuming every microbe needs oxygen - many are harmed by it. Exit ticket: (a) What molecule makes up most bacterial cell walls? (b) In which growth phase do cells divide fastest? Answers: (a) Peptidoglycan. (b) The exponential, or log, phase.

questions.prompt: Van Leeuwenhoek is remembered for...
options: first observing microorganisms with a microscope
questions.explanation: His handmade microscopes revealed the first 'animalcules' in the 1670s.

questions.prompt: The germ theory of disease holds that...
options: illness comes only from an imbalance of humors
many diseases are caused by microorganisms
questions.explanation: Pasteur and Koch established that microbes cause many diseases and can spread.

questions.prompt: Which group is NOT made of cells?
questions.explanation: Viruses are acellular packages of genetic material in a protein coat.

questions.prompt: Prokaryotic cells are defined by...
questions.explanation: Bacteria and archaea keep their DNA in a nucleoid, not a true nucleus.

questions.prompt: During the exponential phase of growth, a bacterial population...
questions.explanation: The log phase is rapid, regular doubling while resources are plentiful.

questions.prompt: A facultative anaerobe...
options: can grow with or without oxygen
questions.explanation: It uses oxygen when present but can also switch to anaerobic metabolism.

lessons.title: Controlling microbes and microbial genetics
lessons.grammar_note: 'Sterilization' kills or removes all microbes; 'disinfection' and 'antisepsis' reduce them but do not guarantee zero. The suffix '-cidal' means it kills; '-static' means it only stops growth.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Choose the right method to control microbes - sterilization, disinfection, or antisepsis - and explain how bacteria share genes without reproducing. You will be able to connect gene sharing to the spread of drug resistance. Warm-up: what is the difference between killing microbes and merely slowing them down?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Controlling microbes means removing, killing, or slowing them to keep food, surfaces, and bodies safe. Sterilization destroys or removes all living microbes, including tough bacterial spores; disinfection lowers microbe numbers on nonliving surfaces; antisepsis does the same on living tissue, such as skin. Methods split into physical and chemical. Heat is the workhorse: the autoclave uses pressurized steam at about 121 degrees Celsius to sterilize instruments, while pasteurization uses milder heat to cut numbers in food. Filtration removes microbes from liquids and air, and radiation such as ultraviolet light damages their genetic material. Chemical agents include alcohols, chlorine, iodine, and hydrogen peroxide. On the genetics side, bacteria carry a single chromosome but can also pick up new genes without ordinary reproduction. This horizontal gene transfer lets traits, including resistance to drugs, spread quickly across a population and even between species.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: There are three main routes of horizontal gene transfer. In transformation, a cell takes up free DNA released by dead cells in its surroundings. In transduction, a virus that infects bacteria, called a bacteriophage, accidentally carries bacterial DNA from one cell to the next. In conjugation, two cells connect through a pilus and pass a plasmid directly, often one that carries resistance genes. Mutations add further variation when DNA is copied imperfectly. For control, matching the method to the job matters: an autoclave for surgical tools, boiling or chemical tablets for water, alcohol rubs for hands, and chlorine for pool water. A product labeled bactericidal kills bacteria, while a bacteriostatic one only halts their growth, leaving time or the immune system to finish the task. Spores are the hardest targets, which is why true sterilization needs intense heat or strong chemical treatment.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which process destroys even bacterial spores? 2) Name the three routes of horizontal gene transfer. 3) What does an autoclave use to sterilize? 4) What is the difference between a bactericidal and a bacteriostatic agent? 5) Why is horizontal gene transfer a concern for antibiotic resistance? Answers: 1) Sterilization, for example by autoclaving. 2) Transformation, transduction, and conjugation. 3) Pressurized steam at high temperature, about 121 degrees Celsius. 4) Bactericidal kills bacteria; bacteriostatic only stops them from multiplying. 5) It lets resistance genes jump quickly between cells and even between species.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: treating 'disinfected' as 'sterile' - disinfection reduces microbes but may leave spores alive. Mistake: thinking bacteria can only pass genes to their offspring; horizontal transfer moves genes sideways between unrelated cells. Exit ticket: (a) Which is stronger, sterilization or disinfection? (b) Name the transfer route that uses a bacteriophage. Answers: (a) Sterilization, which removes or kills all microbes including spores. (b) Transduction.

lessons.title: How microbes cause disease; immunity and vaccines
lessons.grammar_note: A 'pathogen' is a microbe that causes disease; 'virulence' is how severe or damaging a pathogen is. Not every microbe in or on us is a pathogen.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how pathogens cause disease, describe in brief how the body defends itself, and say how vaccines prepare that defense in advance. You will be able to tell innate from adaptive immunity. Warm-up: why can the same microbe make one person very sick and barely affect another?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Only a minority of microbes are pathogens, able to cause disease. To do so a pathogen must enter the body, attach to and often invade host cells, obtain nutrients, and evade defenses. Virulence - the degree of harm a pathogen causes - depends on virulence factors such as capsules that resist being engulfed, enzymes that break down tissue, and toxins. Exotoxins are proteins released by bacteria, while endotoxins are parts of the outer membrane of certain bacteria that trigger strong inflammation. Damage can come from the microbe directly or from the body's own overreaction. Against all this the host has layers of defense. Innate immunity acts fast and the same way every time: skin and mucous barriers, inflammation, and white blood cells that engulf invaders. Adaptive immunity is slower but specific: it recognizes a particular microbe and remembers it, so a second exposure is met quickly and strongly.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: The adaptive response centers on lymphocytes. B cells make antibodies, proteins that bind a specific target called an antigen and mark it for destruction or neutralize it. T cells kill infected cells and coordinate the response. After an infection clears, memory cells remain, giving lasting immunity to that microbe. Vaccines use this memory on purpose. A vaccine presents a harmless form of a pathogen - a weakened or killed microbe, a piece of it such as a surface protein, or instructions for the body to make that piece - so the immune system builds memory without the illness. Later, if the real pathogen arrives, the response is fast and strong. Examples include vaccines against measles, tetanus, polio, and influenza. When enough of a population is immune, spread slows and even unvaccinated people gain some protection, an effect called herd immunity. Pasteur's early rabies and anthrax vaccines were first steps on this path.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is a pathogen? 2) Give two examples of virulence factors. 3) How does innate immunity differ from adaptive immunity? 4) What do B cells produce, and what do those products do? 5) In one sentence, how does a vaccine work? Answers: 1) A microbe that can cause disease. 2) Any two of: capsules, tissue-degrading enzymes, exotoxins, endotoxins. 3) Innate immunity is fast and general; adaptive immunity is slower, specific, and has memory. 4) Antibodies, which bind a specific antigen to neutralize it or mark it for destruction. 5) It exposes the immune system to a harmless form of a pathogen so memory forms without illness, enabling a fast response later.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: assuming every microbe in the body is harmful; most are harmless or helpful, and pathogens are the exception. Mistake: thinking a vaccine gives you the disease; it uses a harmless form to train the immune system. Exit ticket: (a) What does 'virulence' mean? (b) What is herd immunity? Answers: (a) How severe or damaging a pathogen is. (b) When enough of a population is immune that spread slows, protecting even those who are not immune.

lessons.title: Antibiotics, resistance, and applied microbiology
lessons.grammar_note: 'Antibiotic' usually means a drug against bacteria; it does not work on viruses. 'Microbiome' is the community of microbes living in a place, such as the human gut.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain what antibiotics do, why resistance is rising, and how microbes are put to work in the body, in food, in industry, and in the environment. You will be able to say why an antibiotic is useless against a cold. Warm-up: why will an antibiotic not cure a common cold?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Antibiotics are drugs that kill bacteria or stop them from growing, usually by attacking something bacteria have but human cells do not, such as the peptidoglycan cell wall or bacterial ribosomes. The first, penicillin, came from the mold Penicillium, noticed by Alexander Fleming in 1928. Antibiotics transformed medicine, but they do not work on viruses, so they cannot treat a cold or the flu. Their overuse and misuse - stopping a course too early, using them when they are not needed, and heavy use in agriculture - speed up antimicrobial resistance. Resistant bacteria survive treatment and pass their resistance genes on, including by horizontal gene transfer, so once-easy infections become hard to cure. Health agencies call this one of the biggest threats to modern medicine. Meanwhile, most microbes are useful. Applied and environmental microbiology studies how we live with and use them, from the human microbiome to farming, food, and the cycles that keep ecosystems running.

sections.heading: Key methods & examples
sections.text: The human microbiome - the trillions of microbes in the gut and on the skin - helps digest food, makes some vitamins, and crowds out invaders. In food, microbes make bread, cheese, yogurt, beer, and wine through fermentation, and they also cause the spoilage we try to prevent. In industry, engineered microbes produce insulin, enzymes, and other products. In the environment, microbes drive the nitrogen cycle: nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn nitrogen gas from the air into compounds plants can use, while others return nitrogen to the air, keeping soils fertile. Microbes also break down waste in sewage treatment and can clean up pollution, a process called bioremediation. To slow resistance, doctors prescribe antibiotics only when needed, patients are urged to complete courses, and researchers search for new drugs and alternatives such as vaccines and bacteriophage therapy.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Why do antibiotics not cure viral illnesses? 2) Where did penicillin come from? 3) Name two human behaviors that speed up antimicrobial resistance. 4) What do nitrogen-fixing bacteria do? 5) Give one everyday food made with the help of microbes. Answers: 1) Antibiotics target features of bacteria; viruses lack those features and live inside host cells. 2) The mold Penicillium, noticed by Alexander Fleming. 3) Any two of: overuse, using them for viral illness, not completing a course, heavy agricultural use. 4) They convert nitrogen gas from the air into compounds plants can use. 5) Bread, cheese, yogurt, beer, or wine.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: taking an antibiotic for a cold or the flu; these are viral, so the drug does nothing but can still breed resistance. Mistake: thinking the microbiome is harmful; most of its members help us. Exit ticket: (a) What is antimicrobial resistance, in one sentence? (b) Name one beneficial role microbes play in the environment. Answers: (a) When microbes evolve to survive the drugs meant to kill them, making infections hard to treat. (b) Nitrogen fixation, decomposition of waste, or bioremediation of pollution.
